Atlas Resource Policies let Organization Owners constrain the configuration options available to developers when they create or configure Atlas clusters. Atlas uses its own implemented version of Cedar, and only `forbid` policies are accepted ("The converse element, `permit`, is not allowed in Atlas Resource Policies."). Resource policies are evaluated only after RBAC has authorized the request, and are allow-by-default, so they can only forbid actions that the user's role already allows. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-resource-policies.md — https://www.mongodb.com/doc

**In scope.** This report covers how Atlas evaluates Cedar `forbid` policies: the policy object model, the Cedar entity and context vocabulary that Atlas exposes, where evaluation sits relative to RBAC, how Cedar's decision and error semantics apply, how existing and non-compliant resources are treated, validation, and the documented limits.

An Atlas Resource Policy is an organization-level object created with POST /api/atlas/v2/orgs/{orgId}/resourcePolicies. The API has create, list, get, update, delete, validate and non-compliant-resource operations. A policy has a required name, a required org_id and a required policies list whose items each have a Cedar body string, plus an optional description. The server sets id, version, created_date, last_updated_date, created_by_user and last_updated_by_user. Atlas allows only `forbid` policies; the docs say "The converse element, `permit`, is not allowed in Atlas Resource Policies." Atlas's implementation of Cedar supports only one Cedar policy per `.cedar` file, but an Atlas Resource Policy can list multiple `.cedar` files. The `principal` slot is fixed: the docs say "Applied universally by default. Do not change or omit." A policy therefore cannot target or exempt a particular user.
